stimulus.text: The painting shows the Battle of Bunker Hill on June 17, 1775. In the center, the American general Joseph Warren lies dying on the ground, held by a fellow officer. Around him, American militiamen in plain clothes fight hand to hand with British regulars in red coats, who advance from the right under a British flag. At the far right edge stands a Black soldier in the American ranks, musket in hand. The painting is John Trumbull's The Death of General Warren at the Battle of Bunker's Hill, June 17, 1775, painted in 1834, nearly sixty years after the battle.

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: The battle shown in the painting is best remembered because...

options.text: The French army fought alongside the Americans
options.misconception: France did not enter the war until 1778, three years after Bunker Hill; no French troops were there.

options.text: The British won the hill but paid a heavy price in casualties
The Americans held the hill and drove the British back to Boston
options.misconception: The Americans were forced off the hill; the British took it, though at great cost in men.

options.text: The battle was fought at sea, off the Massachusetts coast
options.misconception: Bunker Hill was fought on land outside Boston, on Breed's Hill; no ships or sea fighting are shown.

rationales.B: The British took the hill, but the Americans' fire cost them nearly 1,000 men, a loss that shocked London.
rationales.C: The Americans ran out of ammunition and were driven from the hill; the British held the ground.
rationales.D: The battle was fought on land, on the hills above Charlestown, not at sea.
rationales.A: France entered the war in 1778, after Saratoga; no French soldiers fought at Bunker Hill in 1775.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the center. Warren lies dying and the fighting is hand to hand, so the battle was close and costly.
2. Ask who held the ground. The painting shows the British advancing and the Americans falling back. Background: the British took the hill that day.
3. Weigh the cost. The British won the hill and lost nearly 1,000 men doing it, which told London this war would be expensive.
Remember: a victory can still be bad news — ask what it cost, not just who held the ground. Background: British losses at Bunker Hill were nearly 1,000 men.
